intro: This capstone puts the whole course to work in two ways. First, you become the scientist. With a tape measure, a phone camera, a bubble level and a luggage scale, you measure your own speed, the slope of a path, the friction on a waxed and an unwaxed ledge, the hang time of an ollie and the energy you keep on a ramp. Each test uses the physics from earlier units: speed as distance over time, friction as μ times weight, h = g × t² ÷ 8 for a jump and v = √(2gh) for a drop.

Second, you become an advocate. Most public skateparks exist because a group of ordinary people asked for one, counted who would use it, answered their neighbors' worries and stood up at a city council meeting. You will follow that path from a first sketch to a written proposal, using history from Burnside, the Southbank undercroft and Skateistan, and design ideas that make room for beginners, girls and women, and wheelchair riders.

By the end you will be able to run a simple experiment safely, show every step of the arithmetic, report a result with its uncertainty, and write a proposal that backs each claim with evidence. The two halves meet in the middle: the slope you measure and the sound level you record become facts a council can trust.
bigQuestion: How can careful measurement and steady community work turn skating into knowledge, and a wish into a public place?

title: Capstone: Science and Community

chapters.title: Measure Your Own Skating
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a phone, a tape measure and a notebook turn your own skating into numbers you can trust?

story.title: A Parking Lot Becomes a Lab
story.kicker: On a quiet Sunday, a community class trades guesses for measurements.
paragraphs: The church parking lot is empty by two o'clock on Sunday, and the gate to the street is shut. Renee, who teaches eighth-grade science during the week, unloads a canvas bag from her trunk: a 30-meter tape measure, four orange cones, a roll of blue painter's tape, a bubble level and a spiral notebook. Five adults from her Saturday skate class arrive with boards, helmets and wrist guards.

Marcus, the youngest at 31, asks what they are measuring. Renee hands him the tape. 'You,' she says. 'Your speed, your ollie, your board on a waxed ledge. Today we stop saying fast and high, and start saying how fast and how high.' She has him stretch the tape across the lot and set two cones exactly ten meters apart.

Dolores sets her phone on a backpack well off to the side of the path and switches the camera to 60 frames per second. Marcus rolls through the cones at an easy pace, five times in a row. Between runs, nobody talks about style. They talk about frame numbers, and who wrote down run three.

By four o'clock the notebook holds a column of times, a slope measured with the bubble level and a borrowed one-meter board, the pull on a luggage scale dragging a weighted deck along a portable ledge, and the hang time of Marcus's best flat-ground ollie. Renee does the arithmetic out loud on the hood of her car, step by step, so everyone can check it.

The numbers mostly match the physics they predicted. Where they do not, the group argues happily about why: a crack in the asphalt, a slow thumb on a stopwatch, a wax job that wore off. Renee closes the notebook and says the best part of science is that next Sunday, they can test their arguments.
story.think: What is one thing about your own skating, or a friend's, that you could measure with a tape and a phone, and what would you expect to find?

lessons.title: Speed from Distance and Time
lessons.mainIdea: Average speed is the distance you cover divided by the time it takes, so two marked cones and a clock are enough to measure it.
reading: On an empty, fenced parking lot, Marcus sets two cones exactly 10.0 meters apart with a tape measure. A friend films from the side while he rolls past both cones at an easy pace. The video shows that he took 2.5 seconds to go from the first cone to the second. Those two numbers are all you need to find his *average speed*.

Average speed is distance divided by time. Here it is 10.0 m ÷ 2.5 s = 4.0 *meters per second*, written m/s. To compare with a car's speedometer, multiply by 3.6 to get kilometers per hour: 4.0 × 3.6 = 14.4 km/h. In miles per hour, 4.0 m/s is about 9 mph, a brisk cruising pace on a skateboard.

The word average matters. Marcus may have sped up a little after a push or slowed near the second cone. The calculation gives one number that stands for the whole stretch. A shorter *gate*, the measured gap between two marks, gives a number closer to the speed at a single moment, but it is harder to time well.

Choose a test site with no moving cars, a smooth surface and plenty of room to stop past the second cone. Wear a helmet and wrist guards even for slow test runs, because a pebble can stop a wheel without warning. The person filming stands well to the side of the path, never in front of the rider.

lessons.title: Counting Video Frames
lessons.mainIdea: Counting video frames gives a more exact time than a hand stopwatch, because each frame is a fixed slice of a second.
reading: A stopwatch started by hand is often off by around a fifth of a second, because of *reaction time*, the short delay between seeing something and moving your thumb. Video avoids that delay. Most phones record at 30 or 60 *frames per second*, meaning 30 or 60 still pictures every second. Many free video apps let you step forward one frame at a time.

Here is the method. Step through the clip until the front axle lines up with the first cone, and write down that frame number, for example frame 112. Step on until the front axle reaches the second cone: frame 187. The board took 187 − 112 = 75 frames. At 30 frames per second, the time is 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 seconds.

Each frame at 30 frames per second lasts 1 ÷ 30, or about 0.033 s. That is the *resolution* of your clock, the smallest step it can show. Pick a frame one too early or one too late, and the 2.5 s run could read 2.47 s or 2.53 s. The speed would then shift from 4.0 m/s to about 4.05 or 3.95 m/s. Filming at 60 frames per second halves that step to about 0.017 s.

Use the same part of the board at both cones, such as the front axle, so the distance you measured matches the distance you timed. Check the camera settings before you film, and write the frame rate in your notebook next to the clip's name. A frame rate you guessed wrong would make every time in the test wrong by the same factor.

how many still pictures a video records each second
the smallest step a measuring tool can show; for 30-frame video, about 0.033 s

look.title: Two Paused Frames
look.text: Pause the clip at frame 112. The front axle sits exactly beside cone one. Tap forward, one frame at a time, as the board slides across the screen. At frame 187 the front axle lines up with cone two. Write both numbers in the notebook before doing any math: 187 minus 112 is 75 frames.

check.q: A run starts at frame 40 and ends at frame 100 at 30 frames per second. How long did it take?
check.why: 100 − 40 = 60 frames, and 60 ÷ 30 = 2.0 seconds.

check.q: What is the time resolution of a 60 frames per second video?
check.why: Each frame lasts 1 ÷ 60 of a second, about 0.017 s.

lessons.title: Repeat Runs and Honest Error
lessons.mainIdea: Repeating a test, reporting the mean and the range, and filming from the right spot make a measurement trustworthy.
reading: Where you film from changes what you see. If the camera looks at a cone from an angle, the board can seem to reach the cone before it really has. This is called *parallax*. To shrink it, draw a chalk line straight across the path at each cone and film from far back, so both lines are in view. The farther back the camera, the smaller the angle and the smaller the error.

One run is a story; five runs are data. Marcus rolls through the gate five times and gets 2.5, 2.4, 2.6, 2.5 and 2.5 seconds. The *mean*, or average, is the sum divided by the count: (2.5 + 2.4 + 2.6 + 2.5 + 2.5) ÷ 5 = 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5 s. The mean is a better estimate than any single run, because small timing errors in either direction tend to cancel.

The *range* tells how spread out the runs are. His fastest run was 2.4 s and his slowest was 2.6 s, a spread of 0.2 s. A scientist reports both numbers: about 2.5 s, give or take 0.1 s. That gives a speed of 4.0 m/s, somewhere between about 3.8 and 4.2 m/s.

If one run is far off, such as 3.4 s because a wheel hit a crack, write it down and note what happened instead of quietly deleting it. Decide before the test what rule you will use for leaving out a run, and state that rule in your notes. Choosing the rule after you see the numbers makes it too easy to keep only the runs you like.

the average: the sum of the values divided by how many there are
the spread between the smallest and largest values in a set

check.why: The sum is 12.5 s, and 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5 s.

The board slowing because of friction

lessons.title: Finding the Slope of a Path
lessons.mainIdea: A slope's grade is its rise divided by its run, and on a gentle slope gravity pulls along it with about g times the grade.
reading: Before trusting a speed test on a gentle slope, measure the slope. Lay a straight board exactly 1.00 meter long on the path, lift its low end until a *bubble level* on top reads level, and measure the gap under the lifted end. If the gap is 0.05 m, the path climbs 0.05 m for every 1.00 m across. That is its *rise over run*.

Rise over run is the slope's *grade*. Here 0.05 ÷ 1.00 = 0.05, or a 5% grade. A phone's level app gives the angle instead: a 5% grade is about 2.9 degrees. Road signs in the United States often post steep grades as a percent, so the number matches what drivers already see.

Gravity pulls straight down, but only part of that pull acts along a slope. On a gentle slope that part is about g times the grade: 9.8 m/s² × 0.05 ≈ 0.49 m/s². With no friction, a rider starting from rest would gain about half a meter per second of speed every second. Friction and air take some of that back, which the next test measures.

Do slope tests only on paths closed to cars, such as a park path or an empty lot with a slight tilt. Pick a grade you can already stop on with a foot brake. A gentle grade gives plenty of data, while a steep hill adds speed faster than most riders can control. A street with traffic is never a test site.

the height a slope climbs divided by the flat distance it covers
the steepness of a slope, often written as a percent: rise ÷ run × 100

check.q: With no friction, about how much speed would gravity add each second on a 5% grade?

lessons.title: The Coast-Down Test
lessons.mainIdea: Timing a board's speed and measuring how far it coasts on level ground reveals how strongly rolling losses slow it.
reading: On level ground, a rolling board slowly loses speed even when nobody brakes. The wheels squash a little where they meet the ground, the bearings rub, and air pushes back on the rider. The wheel and ground part of this loss is called *rolling resistance*. A *coast-down test* measures all of these losses together.

Here is the method. Set up the 10 m gate so that its far cone is the start line, on smooth, level pavement. Push to a steady speed, stop pushing before the gate, and stand still on the board as it rolls through. Let it coast until it stops. Measure from the start line to the front wheels with the tape, and use the video to get your speed through the gate.

Suppose the board crosses the line at 4.0 m/s and coasts 40 m. If the slowing is about steady, the *deceleration* is a = v² ÷ (2d) = (4.0 × 4.0) ÷ (2 × 40) = 16 ÷ 80 = 0.20 m/s². Divide by g to compare surfaces: 0.20 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.02. That is an example; your own board, wheels and pavement will give their own number.

Repeat the test with different wheels or on rougher pavement, and compare. Soft wheels, around 78A on the durometer scale, roll over pebbles and cracks but squash more. Harder wheels, near 99A to 101A, usually coast farther on smooth concrete but feel every bump. Change only one thing between tests, so you know which change made the difference.

an experiment that measures how far a board rolls to a stop from a known speed
how quickly something slows down, in meters per second, per second (m/s²)

What should change between two coast-down runs?

The wheels, the rider and the pavement together

check.why: Changing one thing at a time shows which change caused the difference.

check.why: Harder wheels squash less, so they usually roll farther on smooth concrete.

lessons.title: Waxed and Unwaxed Ledge
lessons.mainIdea: Pulling a loaded deck along a ledge with a luggage scale measures the coefficient of friction before and after waxing.
reading: Skaters rub wax on a ledge's edge so boards slide and grind more easily. You can test whether that works with a *luggage scale*, the hand-held kind that hooks to a suitcase and reads its load. Use your own portable ledge or one at a park that allows wax. Wax on public benches and planters makes them slippery for other people and is often against local rules.

Lay an old deck on top of the ledge with its grip tape facing up, so the bottom of the deck touches the ledge as in a boardslide. Add a backpack of books until the deck and load have a mass of 5.0 kg. Hook the scale to a truck and pull slowly along the ledge. Read the scale while the deck slides at a steady pace, not at the first jerk.

Weight is mass times gravity: 5.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 49 N. Most luggage scales read in kilograms, so multiply the reading by 9.8 to get newtons. If the scale reads 2.5 kg on bare concrete, the pull is 2.5 × 9.8 = 24.5 N. The *coefficient of friction* is μ = pull ÷ weight = 24.5 ÷ 49 = 0.50. After waxing, a reading of 1.2 kg gives 1.2 × 9.8 ≈ 11.8 N, and μ = 11.8 ÷ 49 ≈ 0.24. These are example readings.

The extra tug at the very start is *static friction*, the grip between surfaces that are not yet moving. It is usually larger than the *kinetic friction* of surfaces already sliding. That is why a slide can feel sticky as it begins and smoother once it moves. Repeat each test three times, report the mean, and test again after twenty slides to see how quickly the wax wears off.

words.d: a hand-held hook scale that measures how hard you pull, often in kilograms
μ, the friction force divided by the force pressing two surfaces together
the grip that keeps two still surfaces from starting to slide
the friction between two surfaces that are already sliding past each other

look.cite: Worked example: load weight 49 N; example scale readings × 9.8

check.q: A 49 N load needs a steady 24.5 N pull to keep sliding. What is μ?
check.why: μ = pull ÷ weight = 24.5 ÷ 49 = 0.50.

check.q: Why read the scale while the deck slides steadily, not at the first jerk?

The scale only works after a few seconds
Wax only works at the start of a pull
check.why: The starting tug is static friction; the steady pull measures kinetic friction, which is what a slide feels.

check.q: Where is a fair place to wax a ledge for this test?
choices: A city bench outside a library
check.why: Wax makes public benches slippery for others and is often against rules, so use your own ledge or a park that allows it.

lessons.title: Predicting a Slide
lessons.mainIdea: On level ground a slide lasts a distance of v² ÷ (2μg), so lowering friction or adding speed makes it longer.
reading: Once you know μ, you can predict how far a board slides before friction stops it. On level ground, kinetic friction slows a sliding board by μ times g. The *slide distance* is d = v² ÷ (2μg), where v is the speed when the slide begins. Notice that speed is *squared*: double the speed and the slide gets four times longer.

Take a slide that starts at 3.0 m/s on the bare ledge, with μ = 0.50. Then d = (3.0 × 3.0) ÷ (2 × 0.50 × 9.8) = 9.0 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.92 m. On fresh wax, with μ = 0.24, d = 9.0 ÷ (2 × 0.24 × 9.8) = 9.0 ÷ 4.70 ≈ 1.9 m. Cutting μ about in half roughly doubled the slide.

Test the prediction without riding. Use the loaded deck from the luggage-scale test, give it a firm shove along the ledge, and film it beside a tape measure. Count frames over its first 0.3 m to estimate its starting speed, then measure where it stops. Compare that length with d = v² ÷ (2μg).

Real slides rarely match perfectly. The deck may bounce, tilt or hit a rough patch, and μ changes as wax spreads and wears. A *model* is a simple rule that stands in for the real thing. When your measured slide lands close to the prediction, the model is working; when it misses by a lot, something in the setup differs from what you assumed, and that is worth finding.

words.d: how far a board slides before friction stops it: d = v² ÷ (2μg) on level ground
multiplied by itself, as in 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0
a simple rule or equation that stands in for a real situation so you can predict it

look.text: Two shoves send the loaded deck along the freshly waxed ledge. The first starts at 2.0 m/s and stops after about 0.85 m. The second starts twice as fast, at 4.0 m/s. Before you watch the video, use the model: 4.0 × 4.0 = 16, and 16 ÷ 4.70 ≈ 3.4 m.

check.q: In d = v² ÷ (2μg), what happens to the slide if the starting speed doubles?
check.why: Speed is squared, so twice the speed gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the distance.

check.q: A slide starts at 3.0 m/s with μ = 0.50. About how far does it go?
How can you test the slide prediction safely?

Shove the loaded deck by hand and film it
Slide on a wet ledge to go farther
Ask a friend to pull you on the ledge
check.why: Sliding the weighted deck by hand gives the same physics with no rider at risk.

lessons.title: Hang Time from Frames
lessons.mainIdea: The time a board spends in the air sets how high it rose, by the rule h = g × t² ÷ 8.
reading: *Hang time* is how long the board is off the ground during an ollie. Film the trick from the side at 30 or 60 frames per second. Find the last frame where the tail still touches the ground, the moment of *take-off*. Then find the first frame where any wheel lands. If take-off is frame 210 and landing is frame 225, that is 15 frames, or 15 ÷ 30 = 0.50 s.

Gravity alone sets that time. Once the board leaves the ground it is in *free fall*: it rises, slows, stops at the top and falls back. When take-off and landing are at the same height, rising and falling take equal time. So the climb took half the hang time, 0.25 s. An object falling from rest drops a distance of ½ × g × t² in a time t.

Now the height: h = ½ × 9.8 × 0.25 × 0.25 = 4.9 × 0.0625 ≈ 0.31 m. A shortcut does both steps at once with the full hang time: h = g × t² ÷ 8 = 9.8 × 0.50 × 0.50 ÷ 8 = 2.45 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.31 m. A half-second ollie rises about 31 centimeters, close to the length of a school ruler held upright.

Film ollies on flat ground you know well, with your helmet buckled, before measuring anything else. The goal is a clean measurement, not a record. A comfortable ollie you land every time gives better data than a stretch you land once. Ask the person filming to stand to the side, square to the ollie spot, with the whole board in the frame from take-off to landing.

words.d: the time a board or rider spends in the air between take-off and landing
the moment the board leaves the ground, the last frame the tail touches
motion when gravity is the only force acting, as after the board leaves the ground

look.text: Frame 210: the tail strikes the ground and the board points up at a steep angle. Frames 211 to 217: the front foot slides up the grip and the board levels out as it rises. Frame 218: the board hangs at its highest point. Frames 219 to 224: it drops with the rider's knees bending. Frame 225: all four wheels touch down.
look.prompt: If the board leaves at frame 300 and lands at frame 318 at 30 frames per second, what is the hang time?

check.q: An ollie leaves at frame 210 and lands at frame 225 at 30 frames per second. What is the hang time?
Why is the climb time half the hang time?
choices: Rising and falling take equal time when take-off and landing are at the same height
The board falls twice as fast as it rises
The rider pushes the board down halfway
Video cuts the time in half
check.why: In free fall the trip up mirrors the trip down, so each takes half the total time.

check.q: Using h = g × t² ÷ 8, what height matches a 0.50 s hang time?

lessons.title: Checking the Height
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the predicted height with marks on a wall tests the model, as long as you measure the same thing and know your frame error.
reading: A prediction is only useful if you test it. Stick strips of painter's tape on a wall or post behind the ollie spot, one every 10 centimeters from the ground up. In the clip, pause on the highest frame and read where the middle of the deck sits against the marks.

Measure the right thing. The formula gives how far the board's middle rose, not how high the lowest wheel cleared. A board at rest already sits about 10 cm off the ground at its middle, so subtract that *resting height* from the peak reading. If the middle of the deck reaches the 40 cm mark, the *rise* is about 40 − 10 = 30 cm, close to the 31 cm predicted from a 0.50 s hang time.

A single frame matters. At 30 frames per second, counting 14 frames instead of 15 gives 0.467 s and a height of about 0.27 m. Counting 16 gives 0.533 s and about 0.35 m. One frame either way shifts the answer by about 4 centimeters, and that spread is the *uncertainty* of the method. Filming at 60 frames per second makes each frame half as long and cuts the uncertainty roughly in half.

When the two numbers disagree by more than the uncertainty, look for a cause. Landing on a raised surface, or with the board tilted so one truck touches early, changes the time between take-off and landing. Write the cause beside the result instead of forcing the numbers to agree.

how far something climbs above where it started

lessons.title: Energy on a Ramp
lessons.mainIdea: Height becomes speed on a ramp, and comparing the predicted speed with the measured one shows how much energy friction and air took.
reading: A ramp trades height for speed. At the top a rider has *potential energy*, stored by height, equal to mgh. At the bottom that energy has become *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion, equal to ½mv². Set the two equal and the mass cancels, leaving v = √(2gh). A heavier rider and a lighter rider get the same predicted speed.

Take a rider who already drops in comfortably, starting from the *coping* of a mini ramp 1.2 m tall. (Riders still learning can roll down a small bank instead.) The predicted speed at the bottom is v = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.2) = √23.52 ≈ 4.85 m/s. To measure it, tape marks 1.0 m apart on the flat bottom and count frames. If the board crosses 1.0 m in 7 frames at 30 frames per second, that is 1.0 ÷ 0.233 ≈ 4.3 m/s.

The measured speed is lower than the prediction, as it nearly always is. To compare energies in *joules*, take a 70 kg rider. Potential energy at the top is 70 × 9.8 × 1.2 ≈ 823 J. Kinetic energy at the bottom is ½ × 70 × 4.3 × 4.3 = 35 × 18.49 ≈ 647 J. So 647 ÷ 823 ≈ 0.79, or about 79%, of the starting energy showed up as motion.

The missing 176 joules went into rolling resistance, bearing friction, air drag, the sound of the wheels, and the rider's legs, which bend and soak up some energy. The rider's body also does not drop the full 1.2 m, because the center of mass starts and ends above the board. Measuring the gap between prediction and result is how you learn which losses matter most.

lessons.title: Writing It Up Like a Scientist
lessons.mainIdea: A clear report states the question, the hypothesis, the method, the results and a conclusion, so someone else can repeat the test.
reading: A lab report lets someone else repeat your test and check your answer. Start with a clear question, such as: does wax lower the friction on my ledge? Then write a *hypothesis*, a testable guess with a reason: wax will cut μ about in half, because it leaves a slick layer between the deck and the concrete. A hypothesis is useful even when it turns out wrong, because the test still teaches you something.

The *method* lists every step and every measurement so a stranger could repeat it: the 5.0 kg load, the luggage scale, three pulls per surface, the ledge's location and the date. Include a sketch with distances marked. Note anything that might matter, such as the temperature or whether the concrete was dusty.

Results come next: a table of every reading, the mean for each condition and the range. A simple bar chart helps a reader see the difference at a glance. Then the *conclusion* answers the question in one or two sentences and says how sure you are. For example: fresh wax lowered μ from about 0.50 to about 0.24, and the effect faded after twenty slides.

End with what you would change next time and the new question the test raised. Share the report with your crew or class, and invite them to repeat the test with their own boards. When other people get similar numbers, everyone can trust the result more.

the exact steps and tools used in a test, written so others can repeat it
a short answer to the test's question, based on the results, with how sure you are

chapters.title: Plan a Skatepark for Your Town
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it take to turn a town's wish for a skatepark into a safe, welcoming place that gets built?

story.title: From Napkin to Council Chamber
story.kicker: A rough sketch at a diner turns into a plan that a whole town can see.
paragraphs: Lena is a night-shift nurse who started skating again at 38, after her son asked her to teach him. One morning after work, at a diner near the high school, she listens to three teenagers at the next booth. They have been chased out of a grocery store parking lot again. One of them, Andre, pulls a napkin from the holder and starts drawing a bank, a ledge and a little bowl.

Lena leans over and asks if she can add something. She draws a flat area off to one side with a small quarter pipe. 'For beginners,' she says, 'and for people like me.' Andre adds a bench for parents. Before the coffee is gone, the napkin has a parking lot, a path, a light pole and a question mark where the money should go.

Over the next two years the napkin becomes a folder. There are survey results from three schools, a list of 140 people who skate in town, and photos from a skate-a-thon that raised money for the design. A city parks planner joins the group, then a design firm that builds skateparks. At community meetings, children press sticky dots on the features they want most.

On a Tuesday night in spring, Andre stands at a microphone in the council chamber. Behind him, a screen shows a set of real drawings: a plaza section, a bowl, a beginner area with gentle banks, a smooth path from the sidewalk wide enough for a wheelchair, and lights on a timer. He has two minutes. He starts with the napkin.

The vote that night only approves the site. The design and the money will come back at later meetings, and the group will be there for each one. Walking out, Lena tells Andre that most of the work was not the drawing. It was showing up, counting people, answering every worry with a fact and keeping the whole town in the picture.
story.think: If you sketched a skatepark for your own town, who would you invite to help, and what would you draw first?

lessons.title: From Idea to Opening Day
lessons.mainIdea: Most public skateparks are built by cities after advocates show a need, the public helps design it and the council approves the money.
reading: Most public skateparks in the United States start the same way: a group of skaters and parents asks the city for a place to ride. The park is usually built by the city's parks department on public land, with money the city council approves. Between the first request and opening day there are often several years of meetings, planning and fundraising.

The usual steps run in order. First, *advocates*, the people pushing for the park, form a group and show that there is a need. Next, the city looks at possible sites and holds public meetings. Then a *design firm* draws plans and estimates the cost. After that, the city council votes to approve and fund the project, a *contractor* builds it, and the park opens with rules posted.

Many parks today are designed by firms that specialize in skateparks, often started or staffed by skaters. They know how transitions, ledges and flat ground fit together so riders do not crash into each other. Concrete is the usual choice for permanent public parks, shaped by crews who build skateparks, because forming smooth curves in wet concrete takes practice.

This process grew out of hard lessons. Many of the paid parks that opened in the late 1970s, after Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City both opened in 1976, closed in the early 1980s over insurance costs. Free public parks run by cities became common later, as towns worked out *liability*, the question of who is responsible when someone gets hurt.

a company that plans and draws a project and estimates what it will cost

lessons.title: Community Meetings
lessons.mainIdea: At community meetings, skaters and neighbors shape a park's design, and worries answered with facts there are less likely to block it later.
reading: A *community meeting* is where a park's design really begins. The city or the design firm invites skaters, parents, neighbors and anyone else interested. Designers often bring large printouts of the site and let people point, draw and vote on features with sticky dots. Young skaters who are too young to vote in elections can still shape the park here.

Good meetings are planned around the people who will use the park. Holding them after school or on a weekend, near the site, lets students come. A *survey* on paper and online, offered in Spanish or other languages the town speaks, brings in people who cannot attend. Each comment is written down so the next drawing can respond to it.

Neighbors may come with worries about noise, litter, parking or crowds. Answering with facts works better than arguing: show where the nearest homes are, when the lights will switch off and who will empty the trash cans. A worry that is heard and answered at a meeting is less likely to turn into a no vote at the council later.

Most designs go through rounds. The firm presents a *concept design*, a first rough plan, and people react to it. A revised drawing comes back at the next meeting. Skaters who come to every round see their ideas, such as a lower ledge or a small bowl, appear in the plans.

a set of questions asked of many people to learn what they think or need
a first, rough plan shown to the public before the detailed drawings

lessons.title: Budgets and Funding
lessons.mainIdea: A park's budget adds design and a contingency to construction, and the money usually comes from several sources at once.
reading: A skatepark's cost depends mostly on its size and its materials. Here is a worked example: a 1,200-square-meter concrete park at an example price of $500 per square meter. The construction cost is 1,200 × 500 = $600,000. Real prices vary widely by region and year, so a real budget uses local quotes from builders.

Construction is not the whole budget. Design and engineering, permits, lighting, paths, signs and a *contingency*, money held back for surprises, go on top. If design is 10% of construction and the contingency is another 10%, each adds 0.10 × 600,000 = $60,000. That brings the example to $720,000 before lights and paths.

Money usually comes from several places at once. A city's *capital budget*, its plan for long-lasting projects such as parks and roads, often pays the largest share. State park grants, local businesses, service clubs and skater fundraisers fill the gap. The Skatepark Project, founded in 2002 as the Tony Hawk Foundation and renamed in 2020, gives a *grant*, along with advice, to many communities building public parks.

Fundraising also proves support. A council member who sees teenagers running a skate-a-thon knows the park has a real community behind it. Keep a public tally of dollars raised and hours volunteered. Plan for upkeep too: concrete parks need little care beyond cleaning and patching, but someone must budget for it every year.

lessons.title: In Front of the City Council
lessons.mainIdea: The city council decides because it controls the budget, and short, factual public comments help members say yes.
reading: The *city council*, the elected group that governs a town, makes the final decision because it controls the budget. A skatepark usually reaches the council as an item on the *agenda*, the meeting's published list of business. Often a staff report from the parks department explains the site, the design and the cost. Members of the public can usually speak during *public comment*, which is often limited to a few minutes each.

A short, clear talk works best. Say who you are and where you live, state what you are asking for, give two or three facts and thank the council. A student might say how far they now travel to skate, or that they keep getting sent away from parking lots. A parent might describe a child who found friends and exercise on a board. Bring a one-page summary to hand out.

Council members also weigh risk. Some states, including California, have laws that treat skateboarding at a public park as a *hazardous recreational activity*. Such laws limit a city's responsibility when a rider is hurt, especially when rules such as wearing a helmet are posted. Asking city staff how your state handles this answers a common worry before anyone raises it.

A decision may come in steps: first a site, then a design, then the money. Each step is another chance to show up. Steady, polite presence over months often matters more than one big night. Keep a list of which council members asked which questions, and bring an answer to each at the next meeting.

lessons.title: Street Plaza or Bowl
lessons.mainIdea: A street plaza copies city features, a bowl comes from the pool tradition, and many towns mix both in a hybrid park.
reading: A *street plaza* copies the city on purpose: ledges, benches, rails, manual pads, banks and short stairs set in an open, flat space. It grew from the street era of the 1990s, when skaters filmed at real plazas and schoolyards in videos such as Blind's Video Days (1991). A plaza gives street skaters a legal place to practice what they once did on private property.

A *bowl* is a deep, rounded basin with curved walls and a metal or concrete edge along the top. Bowls come from the backyard pools skaters rode during the California drought of 1976–77. Riders carve around the walls, pump through the curves to keep their speed, and do tricks at the lip.

*Transition* is the general word for curved riding surfaces, from small quarter pipes to tall bowls. Many towns choose a *hybrid* park that mixes both styles: a street section, a bowl and smooth banks that link them. Because each area draws different riders, a hybrid spreads people out and serves more ages and styles.

The right mix depends on who will skate there. At the meetings, count skaters by the style they ride and ask where they ride now. A town full of young beginners needs low banks and wide flat ground more than a tall, deep bowl. Skaters who ride both styles can say which features they would use every week, which helps the designers rank them.

a deep, rounded skatepark basin with curved walls, based on backyard pools

lessons.title: Room for Beginners
lessons.mainIdea: A beginner area placed away from fast lines, with features that step up in size, lets new riders of any age learn safely.
reading: Every skilled skater started on a gentle bank. A park built only for advanced riders leaves out children, adults coming back after years, and anyone brand new. A *beginner area* with flat ground, low banks, a small quarter pipe and a low ledge lets people learn pushing, turning, kickturns and a first drop-in without dodging fast riders.

Placement matters as much as the features. Designers think about *lines*, the paths riders take through a park. If the beginner area sits where fast lines cross, collisions follow. Putting it to one side, with clear *sightlines* across it, keeps learners safer and lets parents watch from a bench.

Features can step up in size, such as a 0.6 m quarter pipe, then a 0.9 m one, then a 1.2 m one, so a rider moves up when the last size feels easy. The physics shows why this works: speed at the bottom grows with the square root of height, so doubling the height does not double the speed. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children under 5 should not ride skateboards and that children 6 to 10 should be supervised by an adult, so seating near the beginner area helps grown-ups do that job.

Programs fill a beginner area. Free lesson days, loaner boards and helmets, and quiet morning hours help people who feel nervous in a busy park. Asking beginners at the meetings what would bring them back is a quick way to learn what to build. Adults returning to skating often ask for the same things as children: gentle features, room to fall safely and a little space.

the paths riders take as they move through a skatepark from feature to feature
clear views across a space, so people can see each other and what is coming

look.unit: m/s at the bottom, no friction

check.why: Lines are the routes riders follow from feature to feature.

choices: To keep new riders out of collisions and easy to watch

check.why: Placing it away from fast lines, with clear sightlines, keeps learners safer and lets parents watch.

check.why: Speed grows with the square root of height, so 3.43 m/s becomes 4.85 m/s, not double.

lessons.title: Concrete, Steel and Wood
lessons.mainIdea: Poured concrete lasts longest and is quieter, while prefabricated ramps cost less to start but are louder and wear faster.
reading: Most permanent public parks are poured *concrete*. It lasts for decades and needs little upkeep beyond cleaning and patching. It is also quieter than hollow ramps, because there is no empty space under the surface to drum when wheels roll over it. Concrete costs the most up front and cannot be moved once it has set.

*Prefabricated* ramps are built in a factory from steel, wood or composite panels and set on a flat slab. They cost less to start and can be rearranged. They are louder, because the hollow frame booms like a drum, and their surfaces and fasteners wear and need replacing. Some towns start with prefabricated ramps to show that people will come, then build in concrete later.

The finish matters to the physics. Crews *trowel* concrete smooth so wheels roll with little resistance, and they shape each transition to a steady curve so a rider's path is predictable. A steel pipe along the top edge lets trucks grind smoothly. Ledges often get a metal edge so they stay square after thousands of grinds.

*Drainage* and shade belong in the design too. A flat bottom that holds puddles stays wet for days, and wet concrete is slippery and unsafe to ride. Slopes that carry water to drains, plus shade trees planted where their leaves will not fill a bowl, keep a park usable on more days of the year.

lessons.title: Girls and Women at the Park
lessons.mainIdea: Women have skated from the start, Olympic champions have raised their visibility, and simple design and programs help more girls and women ride.
reading: Women have skated since the sidewalk-surfing days. Patti McGee won the women's national title and appeared on the cover of Life magazine in 1965. Peggy Oki rode for the Zephyr team at the Del Mar Nationals in 1975. Even so, for decades many parks felt like places for boys, and girls often saw no one like them on the ramps.

The Olympics changed what many young riders see. At Tokyo 2020, held in 2021, 13-year-old Momiji Nishiya of Japan won women's street gold, and Rayssa Leal of Brazil, also 13, took silver. Sky Brown of Great Britain, 13, won bronze in park. At Paris 2024, Arisa Trew of Australia won women's park, and Coco Yoshizawa of Japan won women's street. That kind of *representation*, seeing people like yourself succeed, helps new riders picture themselves skating.

Planners can act on this. A weekly girls' and women's *skate night*, women coaches on lesson days, and a beginner area away from the busiest lines help new riders feel welcome. Good lighting, restrooms, seating and clear views across the park are simple features that help many riders feel safe.

*Inclusion* means planning so everyone can take part. Invite girls and women to design meetings directly, through schools, clubs and community groups, not only through skate shops. Their requests, such as a quieter learning space or programs at set times, often help beginners of every gender too.

a set time at a park or rink reserved for a group, such as girls and women
planning a place or program so that everyone can take part and feel welcome

lessons.title: Adaptive Riders and WCMX
lessons.mainIdea: Wheelchair and other adaptive riders use skateparks too, and smooth paths, step-free entries and gentle access ramps let them reach the features.
reading: Skateparks are not only for boards. In *WCMX*, short for wheelchair motocross, riders use sturdy wheelchairs on ramps and in bowls. Aaron Fotheringham, a pioneer of the sport, landed the first wheelchair backflip in the mid-2000s. His riding showed that quarter pipes and bowls work for wheelchairs as well as boards.

*Adaptive* skaters ride in ways that fit their bodies. Some sit on the board, some use a wheelchair, some skate with a prosthetic leg, and some are blind or have low vision and learn a park by sound and touch. Adaptive skate programs lend equipment and teach in small steps, as any good coach does.

A park that welcomes wheelchair riders needs a way in. A smooth, paved path from the sidewalk and parking lot, an *accessible* entrance with no steps, and gentle ramps up to the decks at the top of features let a rider reach the riding areas at all. Transitions with a steady curve, smooth flat bottoms and wide flat ground for turning suit wheelchairs well.

Ask adaptive riders to review the plans, and invite a WCMX rider or an adaptive program to a meeting. The same features that help them, such as gentle access ramps and smooth paths, also help parents with strollers, older visitors and beginners. Planning for access from the first drawing costs far less than adding it after the concrete sets.

lessons.title: Safety, Lighting and Noise
lessons.mainIdea: Clear views, even lighting on a timer and distance from homes make a park safer and quieter, and sound drops about 6 decibels per doubling of distance.
reading: Safe parks are designed, not just posted. Signs typically ask riders to wear helmets and take turns, and list the hours. Open views across the park allow *passive supervision*, the everyday watching that happens when riders, parents and people walking by can see what is going on. A posted street address helps an ambulance find the park quickly.

Lighting adds hours, especially in winter, when it gets dark before many people finish school or work. LED lights on a timer that switches off at closing time can light the riding surfaces evenly without shining into nearby windows. Even light matters, because dark patches hide the cracks and stones that stop a wheel.

Noise is a common worry for neighbors, and physics helps answer it. Sound spreads out as it travels, so it gets quieter with distance. In open air, from a small source, each doubling of distance lowers the level by about 6 *decibels*. If wheels and tails measure 80 dB at 10 m in this worked example, the level is about 74 dB at 20 m, 68 dB at 40 m and 62 dB at 80 m.

Designers use that rule when they place a park. Setting the riding area farther from homes, choosing concrete over hollow ramps, and putting a *berm* or a building between the park and houses all cut noise. A sound meter, or a phone app as a rough guide, can record levels at the nearest home before and after, which gives the council real numbers.

lessons.title: Parks Skaters Built Themselves
lessons.mainIdea: Burnside, the Southbank undercroft and Skateistan show how skaters who build and care for a space can change how a city sees them.
reading: In 1990, skaters in Portland, Oregon, began pouring concrete under the Burnside Bridge without permission. It was a *DIY* park, short for do it yourself. They shaped banks and walls by hand, paid for supplies themselves and kept building. Over time the city accepted the park instead of tearing it out, and Burnside became one of the best-known skateparks in the world.

In London, skaters have ridden the *undercroft* beneath the Southbank Centre since the 1970s. When a redevelopment plan threatened to move them, the Long Live Southbank *campaign* gathered wide public support, and an agreement in 2014 kept the space for skating. The campaign treated a skate spot as part of the city's culture, worth saving like a theater or a gallery.

In 2007, Oliver Percovich founded Skateistan in Kabul, Afghanistan, starting with a few boards and children who gathered to ride. It grew into a skate school that paired skateboarding with classroom lessons, and it welcomed girls, who had few chances to play sport in public. It shows that a skate space can also be a place to learn.

These stories show a pattern useful to any proposal: skaters who show up, build trust and care for a space can change how a city sees them. They also show the limits. Building without permission carries real risks, so most towns now invite skaters into the official process, where the work is legal, inspected and built to last.

lessons.title: Writing the Proposal
lessons.mainIdea: A strong proposal answers the council's questions with evidence: need, site, design, cost, safety and support.
reading: A *proposal* is the written case for the park. A strong one fits on a few pages and answers the questions council members will ask. Why is a park needed? Where will it go, and what will it look like? What will it cost, and who will pay? How will it be kept safe and clean?

*Evidence* makes the case. Count how many people skate in town, with a survey at schools and a sign-in sheet at a skate-a-thon. List where skaters ride now and the problems that causes, such as tickets or close calls with cars in parking lots. Your own measurements help too: the slope of a proposed site from a 1-meter level test, or a sound reading at the nearest home.

Use examples from towns like yours. Find a nearby park of similar size, then ask its parks department how many people use it, what upkeep costs each year and what they would change. Facts from a real neighbor carry more weight than general claims. Attach the design drawings, the budget table and each *letter of support* from parents, teachers, police or local businesses.

Write plainly. Lead with a one-paragraph summary, use headings and put numbers in tables. Thank the people who helped. When the proposal goes to the council, bring skaters of different ages to speak briefly, so members can see the whole community the park would serve.
